account:
Today’s business has been unusually indirect. At the mill I found eighty hay bales available at two emeralds each, but the neighbour reported that builder and freight wanted nineteen bales and offered thirty-two oak planks and services rather than ordinary payment. The innkeeper also urgently needed grain and was considering credit or trade. I later saw builder give planks to baker, which may be part of those arrangements, though I did not witness the terms or any grain delivery.

Several townsfolk have repeated a vague report of a bridge or port change at the bakery. One named baker, innkeeper and freight as having been there, but nobody has yet explained an actual change to me. Repetition is not confirmation. Freight is now at my office and has requested a ferry and warehouse operations discussion at eighteen hundred, in the great hall. That may provide a practical explanation for the waterfront talk. I have accepted it alongside the already scheduled lighting inspection with builder; eight lanterns were reportedly installed for that inspection. I have asked freight what issues and proposed changes I should prepare for, and am awaiting an answer.

There is also unresolved town business: the treasury contains emeralds but I found no account records, and the secretary’s search of the great hall tables produced no records identifying who holds the missing figures. One table chest contained bread. The secretary reports no council correspondence or decisions today and no reliable lead on the accounts. I cannot yet connect those facts to the grain dealings or waterfront rumour.

My best current explanation is that baker, builder, freight and innkeeper are working out supplies and payment through trade or services, with some ferry or warehouse business to discuss this evening. It is possible that something else is being arranged without my knowledge, but I have no evidence of its purpose beyond these reports. I should keep my three o’clock tea with the neighbour, return for the sixteen-thirty office appointment, and attend the eighteen hundred great hall meeting, asking for firsthand details rather than treating rumours as established facts.
